newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-UK Conservative activists want say in new leader.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-UK Conservative activists want say in new leader.

text.p: British Conservative Party members, licking their wounds after humiliation at the polls, are taking up arms again -- against their own members of parliament.
The party is a shambles after its worst election defeat in living memory on May 1 and the battle to find a new leader has disintegrated into vicious bickering among the six candidates.

Feeling let down by their representatives in parliament, grassroots members are demanding a say in who will replace John Major as party leader and lead the counter-attack against Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Major, crushed by the scale of a defeat that ended his party's 18 years in power, wasted no time announcing a day after the election that he would step down.

With just 164 MPs in the 659-seat parliament, no representatives in Scotland or Wales and few in large sections of England, local members argue that the surviving MPs who will choose the next leader are not representative of the party.
They want a change in party rules which would give members throughout Britain a vote for the first time in 160 years rather than it being limited to parliamentarians.
"Letting just 164 MPs choose the next leader would be totally out of order," said Geoffrey Gelberg, a deputy chairman of a local Conservative association.

"In addition to the rump number of MPs, the whole country should have a say. Conservative associations should have the same vote as any member of parliament," the 62-year-old retired lawyer added. Gelberg is not alone.
LEADING MEMBERS CALL FOR CHANGE

High-profile Conservative historian Lord Robert Blake, Robin Hodgson, chairman of the executive committee of the National Union which represents the party's non-parliamentary members, and even some leadership contenders agree something must be done.

"Times have changed and the Conservative Party must change with them. The absence of MPs in large tracts of the United Kingdom has made the need for a review all the more urgent," Blake said in a recent interview.
Under the current system which was instituted in 1965, members of parliament, after consultations with local party members, select the party leader by secret ballot.
The winner will need an overall majority and a 15 percent lead over the closest rival to win on the first ballot.
If goes to a second ballot an overall majority will clinch it, otherwise the two top candidates will fight it out in a third round.

Local activists -- the loyalists who stuff envelopes, make telephone calls and knock on doors canvassing for support -- say it is illogical for only MPs, whose plotting against Major and lack of unity contributed to the election debacle, to decide the next leader.

"There should be a role for volunteers in the party who give their time...weekends, year in, year out. They support the party and they should be entitled to say something about who is the leader of the party," Hodgson said.
Party membership has declined rapidly in recent years and local members feel they were largely ignored, except at election time, by parliamentary deputies grown lazy after 18 years in power.
With the election for Conservative leader due by early summer, Hodgson realises it is unrealistic, if not impossible, to change the rules for a "one person, one vote" in the next two months.
Instead he is organising and planning to publish a grassroots poll which he hopes will force MPs to give local activists 20 percent of the vote for the new leader.

"If the new leader wants to speak for all parts of the United Kingdom it must be helpful for him to have the moral authority from an electoral college which comes from those areas," Hodgson told The Daily Telegraph newspaper.
Under Hodgson's plan, which he says can be in place in time for the leadership poll, 894 leading Conservatives throughout Britain will survey their local members and then vote by phone.

The local results will be kept secret if they are included in the leadership poll. If they are not included, the results will be publicised which could prove highly embarrassing if grassroots support goes against the MPs' choice.
MIXED REACTION TO PROPOSALS FROM LEADERSHIP HOPEFULS
Party chairman Brain Mawhinney, likely to step down after a new leader is chosen, believes local parties should be given a say in choosing a new leader, perhaps 15 percent of the vote.
Reaction to the proposal from the leading contenders has been mixed.

William Hague, the former Welsh minister and favourite to succeed Major, is said to favour including grassroot members as does ex-finance minister Kenneth Clarke and Stephen Dorrell who was previously in charge of the Department of Health.
But John Redwood, a leading Eurosceptic who lost the battle for the party's top job to Major in 1995, does not.

"Mr Hodgson's proposals are being rushed through far too quickly, in the midst of a vacuum of authority -- the worst conditions in which to change the rules of the game," argued The Daily Telegraph in an editorial.
"These ought to be considered not in isolation, but rather as part of an overall package of reforms."
Whatever the final decision on the voting structure, most Conservatives agree the party is in need of an overhaul if it is to remain a credible force in British politics.
The Conservative vote fell to 9.6 million in this month's election from 14 million in 1992 with more than three million voters switching away from Major's party.

Even before the election the Conservatives, traditionally strong at local level, had less local councillors than either Labour or the Liberal Democrats, whose strong organisation at local level puts the Conservatives to shame.
